title: Human-induced climate change intensifies spatially compounding fire weather extremes across European countries
abstract: Abstract Intensifying fire weather extremes increasingly threaten Europe, with recent wildfires linked to human-induced climate change. Yet, little is known about spatially compounding fire danger events—days when multiple regions simultaneously face extreme fire weather—which can trigger widespread fires and potentially overwhelm shared EU firefighting resources, amplifying impacts. Here, we analyse spatially compounding fire danger by combining burned area observations (2001–2015), ERA5-based Fire Weather Index data (1950–2024), and CMIP6 climate simulations. We reveal that cross-country correlations in fire weather strongly enhance the likelihood of extremely widespread fire weather events, with these events primarily driven by long-lasting compound hot-dry meteorological conditions. The spatial extent of extreme fire weather has expanded markedly over the past three decades, primarily due to rising temperature and the associated decline in relative humidity. On average over the past decade, human-induced climate change contributed to the annual-maximum extent of European land synchronously experiencing extreme fire weather by 14.8% (4.8–25.6%, interquartile range across models). These results highlight the need for coordinated European adaptation to the growing potential for large-scale wildfires.
problem: Existing knowledge is limited regarding spatially compounding fire danger events—when multiple regions simultaneously face extreme fire weather—which can overwhelm shared firefighting resources and hinder the assessment of risks for large-scale wildfires.
method: The authors propose a method that analyzes spatially compounding fire danger by integrating burned area observations, ERA5 reanalysis, and CMIP6 climate models, using a detrending approach to quantify the contribution of human-induced climate change to recent trends.
task: The task is to analyze spatially compounding fire danger events across Europe by combining observations, reanalysis, and climate simulations to quantify recent trends, drivers, and the contribution of human-induced climate change.
innovation: This paper reveals that human-induced climate change has intensified spatially compounding fire weather extremes across European countries, primarily driven by rising temperatures and declining relative humidity, expanding their average annual-maximum extent by 14.8% over the past decade.

Across the continent, climate change is projected to intensify FWI extremes, particularly in southern Europe, with rising temperatures and decreasing relative humidity contributing to longer fire seasons and more frequent FWI extreme events.

For Europe, Torres-Vázquez et al. analyzed historical trends and explored the future response of synchronous FWI extremes across individual European IPCC regions to spatially uniform perturbations in temperature and pre-cipitation, identifying Central Europe as a hotspot of increasing fire weather synchronicity.

Regions such as Western and Central Europe, historically less affected by extreme FWI conditions, may be drawn more frequently into large-scale events as the spatial extent of extreme fire weather expands, posing new challenges for fire management systems.

To respond more effectively to disasters such as wildfires, 37 countries cooperate through the EU Civil Protection Mechanism, which enables the sharing of firefighting aircraft, personnel, and medical support.

Fig. 5 | Effect of human-induced climate change on spatially compounding fire danger over Europe. a Contribution of climate change (%), arising from changes (relative to 1850-1900) in different meteorological drivers, to the annual-maximum extent of European land under fire weather extremes (averaged across annual maxima over 2014-2024). Bars show the multi-model mean across 17 CMIP6 climate models, black whiskers indicate the interquartile range, and gray dots represent individual model values outside that range (one value per model). b Same as (a), but for the linear trend of these climate change contributions over 1994–2024 (see “Methods”). c Temperature change relative to 1950–1980 for ERA5 (black) and all ensemble members for CMIP6 models (in colors). Each color is associated with an individual model. d Annual climate change contribution (%) since 1850–1900 from temperature trends to the extent of European land under extreme fire danger con-ditions. The legend shows the datasets used, with the number of ensemble members indicated in parentheses.
